tldr: We present a system where a robot arm autonomously performs chemistry experiments on a bench set up for humans, telling containers apart by reading their labels and working directly from a photo of a printed instruction sheet.
hero_caption: Overall workflow of Curie's Jarvis. (A) A VLM extracts steps and creates a plan from a photo of the instruction sheet. (B) Container paper labels are identified via majority voting across four camera views. (C) The bench is reconstructed from 3D point clouds to locate objects. (D) The robot arm executes skills with dynamically tuned parameters.
overview:
Traditional lab automation systems usually follow pre-programmed procedures using dedicated scripts, relying on fixed equipment racks or fiducial markers like AprilTags. Human researchers, on the other hand, read printed protocol sheets, distinguish identical cups by handwritten labels, and check the bench before each step to adapt on the fly. Rebuilding human-oriented laboratory environments exclusively for robots significantly undermines experimental flexibility.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed "Curie's Jarvis," a chemistry robot that behaves like a human experimenter. The system reads protocols directly from photos of color instruction sheets found in children's chemistry kits, and it uses four camera views to read labels (both printed and handwritten) on the bench to tell identical containers apart. Furthermore, it re-verifies container locations immediately before each step and adjusts motion parameters—such as carrying liquid-filled containers at lower speeds.

In real-robot evaluations using a Franka Emika Panda, the system completed 9 out of 10 runs without human intervention across two chemistry experiments (Magic Beaker and jellyfish). Additionally, it achieved a 100% success rate across 160 container locate trials on handwritten and printed labels. This represents a practical and important step toward bringing robots into laboratories built for humans.
contributions: Demonstrated fully autonomous experiments on an ordinary bench without markers or fixed fixtures, understanding tasks directly from photos of printed protocol sheets.
Achieved 100% accuracy across 160 trials identifying identical containers with handwritten and printed labels using cross-camera voting and multi-view geometry.
Built a robust pipeline that relocates targets visually right before each step, allowing the system to track containers even if moved by a human between steps.
Realized adaptive parameter control that adjusts execution speed, tilt angles, and scoop depth based on protocol instructions and the state of handled materials (empty, powder, liquid).

sections.heading: Five properties to adapt robots to human lab benches
sections.summary: Humans read paper protocols, identify haphazardly placed labeled containers, and work carefully based on their contents. This study defines five requirements for robots to achieve that human-like flexibility.
sections.details:
Picture a student running a bench experiment. They lay out a printed protocol sheet, place beakers with handwritten labels in empty bench spaces, and visually check the bench before moving their hands. They carry empty containers quickly, but move full liquid containers slowly to avoid spills. In contrast, existing lab automation systems force the entire environment to adapt to the robot—requiring dedicated scripts, rigidly fixed equipment, and fiducial markers like AprilTags.

Curie's Jarvis is proposed to bridge this divide. To adapt the robot to human-centric laboratory environments, it was designed to satisfy five properties (P1–P5):
- (P1) Starts from a photo of a printed protocol sheet without manual scripting.
- (P2) Operates on an ordinary bench without fixed fixtures or markers.
- (P3) Tells visually identical containers apart using handwritten or printed labels.
- (P4) Relocates targets right before each step, finding objects even if moved.
- (P5) Adapts speed, pour angle, and scoop depth according to instructions and contents.

Using a Franka Panda arm, the system completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol and 4 of 5 runs of another from a children's chemistry kit, correctly identifying the target container in all 160 out of 160 label recognition trials.

sections.heading: The current state of lab automation and language models
sections.summary: Most automated labs rebuild the environment around the robot, sacrificing flexibility. While language models are increasingly adopted, no prior system could run directly from paper protocols, read labels, and adapt to dynamic benches.
sections.details:
Research into laboratory automation has a long history, but its reliability has traditionally relied on structuring the environment. For example, robots touch calibration cubes to align within 0.12 mm, or every piece of labware is tagged with QR codes or AprilTags. However, this approach requires precise marker offset calibrations for every setup, creating heavy operational overhead.

Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been used to generate experimental procedures from natural language. A closely related system is ORGANA, which recognizes transparent glassware without markers; however, it requires users to manually assign the roles of identical containers upfront and cannot replan online if a human moves items mid-procedure.

Furthermore, LLM applications in robotics have expanded from simple skill sequence generation to parameter tuning, such as adjusting execution speed and selecting contact forces. Curie's Jarvis builds on these ideas by integrating VLM-based label reading, multi-view geometric localization, and dynamic context-dependent motion parameter tuning.

sections.heading: Hardware setup and modularized agents
sections.summary: A Franka Panda arm and four RealSense cameras work alongside four GPT-4.1-based agents and SAM 3 in a modular system architecture.
sections.details:
Curie's Jarvis cleanly separates responsibilities across hardware and software.

The hardware consists of a 7-DoF Franka Emika Panda arm equipped with a Franka Hand parallel gripper. A cage surrounding the bench holds four Intel RealSense D415 RGB-D cameras capturing the workspace from different angles. The bench holds common equipment: white reagent bowls, transparent plastic cups, beakers, pipettes, and 3D-printed spoons and stirring rods.

The software is divided between a GPU server running the open-vocabulary segmentation model SAM 3 and the main robot control program. The LLM side is modularized into four agents (all running GPT-4.1):
- Instruction Parser: Extracts goals, steps, reagents, and equipment from instruction sheet photos (run once at startup).
- Scene Agent: Matches camera images against the list of bench items to identify names (run once at startup).
- Planner: Decomposes the overall goal into subtasks and handles replanning upon failure.
- Skill-call Agent: Outputs predefined manipulation skills (pour, scoop, etc.) and runtime parameters in JSON format based on gripper status.

Each skill independently handles perception and grasp planning, verifying that goals are reached during execution.

captions.F2: Curie's Jarvis system architecture. The top-left blue box (instruction parsing, scene recognition, global planning) runs once at the start. The top-right orange box (skill call) and bottom orange box (perception and skill execution) repeat for each subtask.

sections.heading: Reliable object recognition via multi-view geometry and label voting
sections.summary: SAM 3 extracts masks from four camera views. Opaque containers are located via depth point clouds, while transparent containers use ray intersection. Identical containers are distinguished by majority voting on paper labels across all views.
sections.details:
The robot is not given object coordinates; it only receives a list of items present on the bench. Accurately locating them is the core perception challenge.

### IV-A Open-Vocabulary Segmentation and 3D Integration
First, SAM 3 receives a text prompt like "white bowl" to obtain masks across all four camera views. For opaque objects, depth point clouds from each mask are back-projected into the robot frame, and views with centroids within 50 mm are merged. If views disagree, both are discarded to prevent false detections.

In contrast, depth point clouds fail for transparent cups because the IR light passes through the container and measures the bench surface (causing centroid errors up to 6 cm in experiments). To solve this, rays are cast from mask centroids in each camera, finding the intersection point where rays pass within 25 mm of each other within the container's height bounds. Empirically, this error stays within 6–11 mm. Placing a pre-registered cylindrical model at that intersection enables successful grasping.

### IV-B Reading Human-Written Labels (P3)
To tell identical cups and bowls apart, a paper slip (label) is placed under each container. For each camera, the VLM inspects a crop showing the container and the paper underneath, choosing from candidate labels on the bench.

Because a single camera can miss or misread text due to steep angles, a four-camera voting scheme is used. The label assignment with the most matching views is selected. If ambiguous, the system resolves it by elimination (when all other containers are assigned and one matches). If the container was previously moved by the robot itself and no longer sits on its paper, any container within 50 mm of the previous drop-off location is treated as that object.

captions.F3: Example of a single localization process on the real robot. (a) SAM 3 extracts object masks from four camera views, (b) the VLM reads labels in each view for majority voting, and (c) multi-view geometry estimates the precise 3D position.

sections.heading: Robust manipulation skills that detect failures and retry
sections.summary: A fixed skill set covers grasping, scooping, pouring, stirring, and pipetting. Each skill relocates targets from a home position and monitors failures via contact force and gripper width.
sections.details:
Every skill follows a shared pipeline. First, the arm retreats to a home position clear of camera views and re-identifies the target from fresh frames. It plans and executes trajectories using measured geometry, then checks if it reached the target and verifies gripper width to ensure objects were neither dropped nor crushed.

- Grasping: Executes a top-grasp at the point cloud center. Rigid tools close until reaching a set gripping force, whereas thin plastic cups use position control, closing slightly past the measured width for a gentle grip. Gripper width before and after lifting detects misses, crushed cups, or slippage.
- Scoop and Dump: Depth data detects powder surface height. The spoon makes gentle surface contact before descending to a target depth, staying level while lifting to avoid spilling. If stuck, it retries at a shallower depth. Over the target cup, the spoon tilts and executes small shakes to empty all powder.
- Pour: The gripped cup rim overlaps inside the target cup rim based on grasp measurements. The wrist incrementally tilts toward the target angle while adjusting position. If pouring is incomplete, it slows down and retries.
- Stir and Tool Return: The stirring rod descends vertically, tracing a circular path sized to the cup rim without scraping the walls. Used tools return to their initial pickup positions.
- Pipette: The bulb of a pipette standing in a paper cup is squeezed by the gripper, submerged into liquid, and released slightly to draw up liquid before dispensing drops.

sections.heading: Turning instruction photos into safe robot actions
sections.summary: A VLM extracts steps from the instruction sheet, and the planner expands them into subtasks. The skill-call agent enforces a strict JSON schema to produce valid executable parameters.
sections.details:
The pipeline converting photos into robot actions incorporates deliberate guardrails against LLM hallucinations.

First, the instruction parser processes the sheet photo to extract goals, steps, reagents, and equipment in JSON. Prompting the parser to strictly retain original container names and quantities proved essential. Without this constraint, an "empty transparent cup" was misread as a "beaker" in 2 out of 3 runs; with it, extraction succeeded in 3 out of 3 runs.

The planner then breaks these instructions into a subtask list (around 30 for Magic Beaker, 20 for jellyfish) following constraints such as "a scoop skill must always be followed by a dump skill" and "numbered steps must run sequentially."

The skill-call agent handles subtask execution. Outputs are strictly constrained by a JSON schema containing only predefined skill names, target containers, speeds, and brief rationales. If a subtask cannot be performed by the current skill set, rather than forcing an improper skill, it returns "infeasible" to prompt replanning. Tool CAD models and scoop depths that the model cannot know are populated automatically from hardcoded values and grasp measurements.

sections.heading: Real-robot experiments: High success rate and flawless label identification
sections.summary: Across 10 runs of two chemistry protocols, 9 completed without human intervention. In 160 label identification trials, multi-view voting achieved a 100% success rate across printed and handwritten labels.
sections.details:
### VII-A Experimental Setup and Protocols
Two protocols from a commercial children's chemistry kit (National Geographic Kids) were used: (1) Magic Beaker: Citric acid and baking soda dissolve in separate water cups, cabbage powder indicator turns them red and blue, and mixing them yields fizzing and purple color. (2) jellyfish: Cooking oil is poured over baking soda solution, and cabbage indicator dropped via pipette sinks through the oil and turns blue in the basic water layer. Each protocol was tested 5 times on the real robot.

### VII-B End-to-End Execution from Sheets (P1, P2)
Magic Beaker succeeded in 5/5 runs (~30 min each), and jellyfish succeeded in 4/5 runs (~17 min each). All successful runs showed the expected visual color changes and fizzing described in the protocols.
The single failure occurred on jellyfish's final step: when attempting to grasp the pipette, the robot misidentified a differently shaped spoon as the pipette. Because tools are identified by appearance without labels using SAM 3 text prompts, the segmentation error caused immediate failure.

### VII-C Container Identification via Labels (P3)
Four containers (cabbage bowl, baking soda bowl, water cup, oil beaker) were placed on the bench to evaluate label recognition. Testing printed labels and three handwriting styles across 10 trials each (160 total locate trials) yielded 100% correct identifications, with mean position error of 0.2 mm (max 1.1 mm).
Camera voting was critical: single cameras misread labels in 21 of 160 trials, but the remaining three cameras outvoted errors. Relying on a single camera would have degraded success significantly.
In offset tests placing containers 2–44 cm from paper slips, labels were read reliably as long as containers touched or overlapped the paper. Separating them by an open gap caused failures, showing that local proximity between text and container determines success.

### VII-D & E Robustness to Disturbance and Adaptive Speed (P4, P5)
Because the robot returns to home and re-identifies targets before each step, it handles bench rearranging by humans between steps. Motion speeds (0–100) are assigned dynamically: liquid-filled containers at 0 (slowest), powder spoons at 20, stirring at 30, empty tools at 60, and unladen moves at 80, balancing spill prevention and task speed.

sections.heading: Absence of precision measurement and hardware bottlenecks
sections.summary: Reagents were pre-portioned, as exact measurement is not yet implemented. Furthermore, sequentially querying the four cameras creates perception latency that must be resolved.
sections.details:
The primary limitation of this work is the lack of precision measurement. The protocols tolerated minor measurement variations, and reagents were pre-portioned into small dishes like cooking prep. In real chemistry, milligram or microliter accuracy is required, but this system lacks analytical balances or liquid volume feedback.

A hardware bottleneck also arose: due to USB controller bandwidth limits and GPU memory constraints on the PC, streaming four RealSense cameras and running concurrent segmentation was not possible. Cameras were started, captured, and stopped sequentially before running SAM 3 and the VLM, taking an average of 14.1 seconds per target localization. Much of Magic Beaker's execution time across ~30 steps was spent waiting for vision, highlighting the need for parallel-processing hardware.

Finally, keeping tools unlabelled means that open-vocabulary segmentation errors—such as mistaking a spoon for a pipette—lead directly to unrecoverable system failures.

sections.heading: Advancing robotics toward human-like experimentation
sections.summary: The system demonstrates autonomous chemistry experiments directly from printed sheets on human-style benches. Future work will test real-time disturbances and advanced protocols with precision dispensing.
sections.details:
Curie's Jarvis demonstrates a paradigm shift in laboratory automation: adapting robots to environments and protocols designed for humans. Instead of relying on hardcoded scripts and specialized markers, the robot reads paper instructions, identifies handwritten labels, and inspects the workspace before every action—closely mirroring how a human researcher works.

Achieving 9 out of 10 end-to-end experiment successes and 100% label recognition across 160 trials validates this approach. Future work will focus on evaluating real-time human disturbances during execution, benchmarking fixed versus adaptive speeds, and scaling to high-precision dosing protocols required in drug discovery and materials science.

takeaways: Demonstrates that "adapting the robot to the human environment" (via VLM label reading and multi-view geometry) is a viable alternative to "adapting the environment to the robot" (markers and rigid fixtures).
Single-view VLM label reading fails frequently due to lighting and angles; combining cross-camera voting with process-of-elimination provides practical robustness.
Solves transparent container depth estimation failures (caused by light pass-through) using multi-view ray casting from mask centroids.
Maintains system reliability by using LLMs/VLMs only for high-level planning and parameter selection (speeds, angles), while assigning motion trajectories and contact checks to deterministic skills.
limitations: Reagents were pre-portioned, lacking closed-loop feedback or precision measurement with analytical balances and pipettes.
Sequential image capture and inference across four cameras takes ~14 seconds per step, making total experiment time long.
Tools rely entirely on open-vocabulary appearance prompts without labels; segmentation confusion causes unrecoverable grasp failures.
Dependency on a hosted VLM (GPT-4.1) requires continuous network connectivity and leaves the system vulnerable to model API behavior shifts.
